facts.statement: Acaenasuchus lived approximately 228 to 216.5 million years ago.
facts.quote: Acaenasuchus had a stratigraphic range of approximately 228-216.5 million years ago.

facts.statement: The holotype of Acaenasuchus, a left dorsal paramedian scute, was discovered by Charles Lewis Camp in 1930.
facts.quote: The holotype, UCMP 139576 (a left dorsal paramedian scute), was first discovered by Charles Lewis Camp in 1930.

facts.statement: Robert A. Long and Philip A. Murry established Acaenasuchus as a distinct genus in 1995.
facts.quote: UCMP 139576 was eventually moved into its own taxon and classified under the name Acaenasuchus, upon reclassification by Robert A. Long and Philip A. Murry in 1995.

facts.statement: The species name geoffreyi honors Geoffrey Long for his patience while his father was working in the field.
facts.quote: The species epithet Acaenasuchus geoffreyi was named after Geoffrey Long, Robert A. Long's son, for his "considerable patience while his father was away in the field".

facts.statement: Besides the holotype, 95 other scutes are likely attributed to Acaenasuchus.
facts.quote: In addition to the holotype UCMP 139576, 95 other scutes under 90 catalogue numbers likely also belong to Acaenasuchus.

facts.statement: A specimen known as SMU 75403, described in 2020, includes cranial, vertebral, and appendicular elements along with new variations in the carapace and shield.
facts.quote: Another specimen, known as SMU 75403, was described by Marsh et al. (2020), and consists of representative cranial, vertebral, and appendicular elements as well as previously unknown variations in the dorsal carapace and ventral shield.

facts.statement: Acaenasuchus was a very small, narrow-bodied animal, hypothesized to be less than 0.6 meters long.
facts.quote: Acaenasuchus was very small and narrow-bodied. It is hypothesized to be less than 0.6 m in length.

facts.statement: Acaenasuchus is characterized by scutes that are highly developed along the pre-sacral series.
facts.quote: Acaenasuchus is characterized specifically by scutes highly developed through the pre-sacral series.

facts.statement: The paramedian scutes of Acaenasuchus feature thornlike processes running parallel along their posterior sides.
facts.quote: These scutes further include the presence of thornlike processes parallel along the side of the posterior region of the paramedian scutes.

facts.statement: Acaenasuchus scutes are highly ornamented with ridges and hollows not found in Desmatosuchus.
facts.quote: Additionally the scutes are described as highly ornamented with ridges and hollows not present in Desmatosuchus.

facts.statement: Until 2016, Acaenasuchus was known only from dermal armor, but excavations that year revealed skull, jaw, and backbone bones.
facts.quote: It was known only by its dermal armor until 2016. The 2016 excavations revealed cranial, mandibular, vertebral, pelvic, etc... bones.

facts.statement: Unlike Desmatosuchus, the paramedian scutes of Acaenasuchus lack a "tongue in groove" articulation with adjacent plates.
facts.quote: Acaenasuchus paramedian scutes do not include the "tongue in groove" articulation with adjacent plates as seen on Desmatosuchus.

facts.statement: Medial and lateral wing-like structures extend from the ridges of the pre-sacral scutes.
facts.quote: Medial and lateral "wing" structures emanate from the ridges of the pre-sacral scutes.

facts.statement: Lateral scutes of Acaenasuchus bear two types of horns: conical horns that curve in multiple directions and are wider than the scutes, and blunt horns with less curvature.
facts.quote: There are two types of "horn" structures observed on the lateral scutes. Conical horns curved dorsally, laterally, and posteriorly… and were wider than the scutes themselves.

facts.statement: Acaenasuchus teeth have rounded tips and broad denticles, similar to those of R. callenderi.
facts.quote: The teeth are described as having a rounded tip similar to R. callenderi, and contain broad denticles.

facts.statement: A large boss forms the dorsal surface of the orbit in Acaenasuchus, possibly representing a fused palpebral bone.
facts.quote: There is a large boss that forms the dorsal surface of the orbit, perhaps representing a palpebral co-ossification to the frontal.

facts.statement: Some researchers suggest that features distinguishing Acaenasuchus from Desmatosuchus might represent ontogenetic variation rather than distinct species traits.
facts.quote: Upon review by Andrew B. Heckert and Spencer G. Lucas, the characters that Long and Murry claim to distinguish between the two species may not represent novel scute features but rather ontogenetic variation.

facts.statement: Heckert and Lucas argue that the pitting on Acaenasuchus scutes indicates it is a juvenile Desmatosuchus.
facts.quote: Heckert and Lucas argue that the visible pits and grooves over the dorsal scutes of Acaenasuchus indicate a juvenile stage of Desmatosuchus development.

facts.statement: Despite debates, most paleontologists currently agree that Acaenasuchus is a valid genus separate from Desmatosuchus.
facts.quote: While studies are ongoing, the majority of working paleontologists agree that Acaenasuchus should retain its status as a valid taxon, independent of Desmatosuchus.

facts.statement: Long and Murry noted that Acaenasuchus possessed teeth described as "ornithischian-like" alongside other unique features.
facts.quote: Long and Murry identified small dorsal plates along the carapace of Acaenasuchus, and identified what they described to be"ornithischian-like" teeth, in addition to a multitude of other proposed synapomorphies.

facts.statement: The carapace of Acaenasuchus was highly flexible due to extensive laminae on its plates, enabling swift and agile movement.
facts.quote: Multiple plates of the carapace include extensive laminae suggesting that the carapace was highly flexible, allowing Acaenasuchus to move swiftly with agility.

facts.statement: Unlike Desmatosuchus, Acaenasuchus lacked caudal armor and pectoral spikes, suggesting a trade-off between defense and mobility.
facts.quote: Caudal armor and pectoral spikes are lost in Acaenasuchus when compared to Desmatosuchus, further suggesting an evolutionary tradeoff between defense and armor in exchange for speed and agility.

facts.statement: The type species A. geoffreyi was named by Long and Murry in 1995 based on dermal armor from the Blue Mesa Member of the Chinle Formation in Arizona.
facts.quote: La especie tipo de Acaenasuchus, A. geoffreyi, fue nombrada por Long y Murry (1995) sobre la base de la armadura dérmica del Miembro Blue Mesa de la Formación Chinle en Arizona.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Acaenasuchus is a juvenile Desmatosuchus or a distinct genus, with researchers citing differences in osteoderm characteristics to argue against synonymy.
facts.quote: Heckert y Lucas (1999, 2000, 2002) consideraron a Acaenasuchus como un juvenil de Desmatosuchus. Sin embargo, Irmis (2005) y Parker (2008) disputaron la sinonimia de Acaenasuchus con Desmatosuchus, señalando diferencias entre los dos en las características de los osteodermos.

facts.statement: Recent studies suggest Acaenasuchus is not an aetosaur but is closely related to non-aetosaurian taxa like Euscolosuchus and Revueltosaurus.
facts.quote: Marsh y col. (2020) describieron un nuevo material que demuestra que Acaenasuchus no es un aetosaurio y, en cambio, está estrechamente relacionado con los taxones no aetosaurianos Euscolosuchus y Revueltosaurus.

facts.statement: A 2020 phylogenetic analysis placed Acaenasuchus as closely related to Revueltosaurus and Euscolosuchus.
facts.quote: In 2020, a phylogenetic analysis found Acaenasuchus to be closely related to Revueltosaurus and Euscolosuchus.

facts.statement: Due to lateral osteoderms on its carapace, Acaenasuchus is classified under the broader clade Aetosauroformes rather than strictly within Aetosauria.
facts.quote: This led to the study concluding that Acaenasuchus should be classified under the more broad clade of Aetosauroformes, due to the lateral osteoderms found on their carapace.

facts.statement: Acaenasuchus, meaning "spine crocodile," lived in North America during the Late Triassic, between 228 and 216.5 million years ago.
facts.quote: Acaenasuchus (nombre que significa "cocodrilo espina") es un género extinto perteneciente al orden Suchia, endémico de lo que ahora es Norteamérica durante el período Triásico, viviendo entre hace 228-216.5 millones de años.

facts.statement: The genus Acaenasuchus was established by Long and Murry in 1995.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Long & Murry 1995

facts.statement: Fossil evidence places Acaenasuchus in the Norian stage of the Late Triassic, from 227.3 to 205.7 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Norian to Norian (227.3 to 205.7 million years ago)

facts.statement: Acaenasuchus is considered a terrestrial organism with little evidence suggesting it had semiaquatic capabilities.
facts.quote: Acaenasuchus was known to be a terrestrial organism, there is little information available that would suggest the Acaenasuchus had semiaquatic potential.

facts.statement: Researchers hypothesize that Acaenasuchus occupied a similar ecological niche to smaller archosaurs of the Late Triassic.
facts.quote: Acaenasuchus is hypothesized to occupy a similar niche to smaller archosaurs of the time.

facts.statement: Acaenasuchus belongs to the clade Pseudosuchia, which represents the crocodilian line of archosaurs.
facts.quote: Acaenasuchus has been organized under the clade Pseudosuchia, the crocodilian line archosaurs.

facts.statement: Irmis assigned Acaenasuchus to the family Stagonolepididae in 2005.
facts.quote: Acaenasuchus was assigned to the family Stagonolepididae by Irmis (2005).

facts.statement: Unlike dinosauriforms, the iliac and ischiadic pedicles in Acaenasuchus are not perforated.
facts.quote: The iliac and ischiadic pedicles are not perforated in Acaenasuchus as they are in dinosauriformes.

facts.statement: The recovered humerus of Acaenasuchus features three bulb-like structures on the humeral head, though the mid-diaphysis is missing.
facts.quote: The humerus has been recovered including all regions but the mid-diaphysis. Three bulb like structures can be observed on the humeral head.

rejected.statement: Acaenasuchus lived in Arizona during the Late Triassic, specifically the Carnian and Norian stages.
rejected.quote: Acaenasuchus is an extinct genus of pseudosuchian, endemic to what would be presently be known as Arizona during the Late Triassic, specifically during the Carnian and Norian stages of the Triassic.

rejected.quote: The lateral scutes are longer than they are wide in Acaenasuchus.
